questions.question: Spotify runs SELECT AVG(rating) FROM Listens over a billion rows. Which storage layout minimizes the IO for this query, and why?
options: Row-oriented, because all columns of each listen are packed together for fast reads
Columnar, because the query only needs to read the rating column's pages and can skip the rest
Row-oriented, because aggregates require reassembling whole rows anyway
Either layout costs the same, since every row must be visited to compute an average
questions.explanation: Columnar storage puts all rating values together, so the aggregate reads one column file and skips user_id, song_id, and listen_time. Row layout would waste roughly 75% of the IO on this 4-column table because every page read drags along the unneeded columns.

questions.question: In a slotted page, each slot stores an (offset, length) pointer to its row. What problem does this indirection solve when a row is updated and outgrows its original footprint?
options: It lets the page compress the row so it never needs to move
It allows the page to move the row internally and just repoint the slot, so external references like (page_id, slot_id) stay valid
It automatically splits the row across two pages without any bookkeeping
It converts the row to columnar format to reclaim the space
questions.explanation: The slot array is a level of indirection: the page can relocate a grown row and update only the slot's offset, so anything outside the page that refers to (page_id, slot_id) never breaks. Nothing about slotted pages compresses rows or changes the layout to columnar.

questions.question: Parquet uses a PAX layout: rows are sliced into ~128 MB row-groups, and columns are stored contiguously inside each group. Why is this preferred over pure columnar (one file per column)?
options: Row-groups compress better than whole-column files, since encoding runs can span group boundaries
Pure columnar cannot store min/max statistics, so predicates can never skip data
A single row stays local (no seek per column), the file count collapses, and footer min/max stats still let queries skip whole row-groups
PAX stores each row twice, once by row and once by column, so every query gets its ideal layout
questions.explanation: Pure columnar wins the scan but makes one row a seek per column and explodes a wide partitioned table into ~100,000 tiny files. Parquet keeps the columnar scan-and-compression win inside row-groups while keeping rows local; the only cost is a sliver of compression because an encoding run cannot cross a row-group boundary (option A has it backwards).

questions.question: Which three techniques combine to let BigQuery turn "scan a petabyte" into a seconds-long query?
options: Columnar storage, heavy compression, and tree-based distributed execution
Row storage, B+Tree indexes, and a large buffer pool
In-memory caching, materialized views, and query rewriting
Hash partitioning, sort-merge joins, and replacement selection
questions.explanation: BigQuery (Dremel) reads only the referenced columns, compresses them heavily (dictionary and run-length encoding), and shards the scan across thousands of on-demand workers whose results bubble up a tree. Indexes and buffer pools are the OLTP toolkit, not what makes Dremel-style analytics fast.

questions.question: At Google, querying web-document trends by Date took hours on the original row-based storage. What was the root cause?
options: The Date column was unindexed, so every query did a binary search per row
Dates compress poorly, so the scans were IO-bound on the Date column itself
Row storage cannot be distributed across multiple workers
Reading the tiny Date field dragged along the megabytes-per-row HTML Body stored in the same rows
questions.explanation: In a row layout, all columns of a record live together, so fetching a few bytes of Date meant reading the heavyweight Body field too — hours of wasted IO at Google scale. Dremel fixed this by storing each column separately so a Date query never touches the Body.

questions.question: ClickHouse's MergeTree sustains ~1M inserts/sec AND ~100 ms analytics on the same Listens table. How does the hybrid design achieve both?
options: It keeps two full copies of the table, one row-oriented and one columnar, and applies every insert to both synchronously
It stores everything columnar but caches the last hour of data in RAM
Fresh writes land as small row-oriented parts for fast inserts, and a background merge converts aged parts into compressed columnar segments for fast scans
It routes OLTP queries to a replica and OLAP queries to the primary
questions.explanation: Age picks the layout: recent data needs fast whole-row appends (row parts), old data needs fast column scans (columnar segments), and a background merge converts between them while one query engine reads both. Synchronously double-writing (option A) would drag inserts down to columnar speeds, which is exactly what hybrid avoids.

questions.question: A 64 GB Listens table must be processed on a machine with 6.4 GB of RAM. What does hash partitioning by hash(user_id) % 16 accomplish?
options: It splits the table into 16 RAM-sized partitions, with all rows for a given user guaranteed to land in the same partition
It sorts the table by user_id so later operators get sorted input
It removes duplicate rows so the table fits in RAM
It builds a 16-bucket index so point lookups become O(1)
questions.explanation: Hashing routes every row with the same key to the same partition number, producing 16 partitions of ~4 GB that each fit in RAM and can be sorted, joined, or grouped independently. Hash partitioning does not sort anything — neighbouring keys scatter across partitions — and it builds partition files, not an index.

questions.question: In BigSort's merge phase with B buffer pages, each merge pass combines only about B−1 runs at a time. Why not all B?
options: One page must be reserved as the output buffer, leaving B−1 pages for run inputs
The last page holds the sort comparator's state
Merging B runs would make the algorithm quadratic instead of O(N log N)
One page is reserved for the write-ahead log so a crash can be replayed
questions.explanation: A k-way merge needs one input buffer per run plus one buffer to accumulate output before flushing it to disk, so B pages of RAM support a (B−1)-way merge. There is no comparator state page or WAL page in the model — the reservation is purely for output.

questions.question: The familiar "BigSort costs 4N" figure is a special case, not the general formula. When is 4N actually correct?
options: Whenever the buffer has at least 3 pages, since a 2-way merge always finishes in one pass
Only when the table is already sorted, so Phase 1 can be skipped
When Phase 2 finishes in a single merge pass, i.e. all Phase-1 runs can be merged at once (roughly N/B ≤ B−1)
Never — the true cost is always 2N because each page is read and written once
questions.explanation: Each pass reads and writes every page (2N), and the general cost is 2N × (1 + ⌈log_(B−1)(N/B)⌉); 4N is the case of one run-building pass plus exactly one merge pass, which requires the run count to fit within a single (B−1)-way merge. With a tiny buffer or huge file, extra merge passes push the cost past 4N — that's why BigSort is O(N log N) in IO, not linear.

questions.question: You BNLJ-join Songs (100 pages) with Listens (10,000 pages) using B = 10 buffer pages. Putting Songs on the outer loop costs 100 + ⌈100/10⌉ × 10,000 = 100,100 IOs. Why is Songs the right choice for the outer table?
options: The outer table is the one that gets a hash table built on it, and small tables hash faster
The number of blocks of the outer table determines how many times the inner table is fully re-scanned, so the smaller table should be outer
The outer table must fit entirely in RAM, and only Songs does
Order doesn't matter — swapping the tables gives exactly the same IO count
questions.explanation: The inner table is re-scanned once per outer block, so minimizing outer blocks (⌈P(outer)/B⌉) minimizes the rescans: with Listens as outer you'd pay 1,000 × 100 = 100,000 scan IOs plus 10,000, totalling 110,000 — 10% worse. BNLJ builds no hash table, and the outer table only needs to fit one block at a time, not entirely in RAM.

questions.question: A query joins Songs to Artists on distance(s.audio_vector, a.style_vector) < 0.2. Which join algorithm can execute this, and why?
options: Hash partition join — hashing the vectors sends similar songs to the same partition
Sort-merge join — sorting by vector distance lets the merge phase find close pairs
Block nested loop join — it evaluates an arbitrary predicate on every row pair, so it handles similarity and range conditions that hash and sort-merge cannot
None — similarity joins require a specialized vector database
questions.explanation: BNLJ compares every pair of rows, so the predicate can be anything: similarity, distance, ranges, or compound conditions. Hash and sort-merge joins fundamentally rely on equality of the join key — hashing a vector doesn't put near vectors in the same bucket, and there is no single sort order that brings all close pairs together.

questions.question: The best-case cost of Hash Partition Join is 3(N+M) + OUT. Where do the three passes over the data come from?
options: Read both tables, sort both tables, then merge them
Hash both tables, verify the hash function is collision-free, then join
Read the smaller table three times while streaming the larger table once
Read both tables to partition them, write the partitions out, then read the partitions back to join in RAM
questions.explanation: Phase 1 reads each table once (1st pass) and writes every row into its partition file (2nd pass); Phase 2 reads each partition pair back to build and probe a hash table in RAM (3rd pass). Sorting is sort-merge join's cost, not HPJ's.

questions.question: During an HPJ of Users and Listens, user_id = 1 (a system account) has 10M listens, so partition 1 overflows RAM while all other partitions fit. What does the algorithm do?
options: Fail the query, since HPJ requires every partition to fit in RAM
Silently fall back to BNLJ for the entire join
Increase the global partition count and re-run Phase 1 on both full tables
Detect the oversized partition and recursively re-partition just that partition with a different hash function until the pieces fit
questions.explanation: Hash skew from hot keys is handled locally: only the overflowing partition is recursively re-partitioned (with a different hash, or handled by a sort-merge fallback), adding an extra pass for that data only. Re-running Phase 1 on everything would waste the work already done on the well-sized partitions.

questions.question: Beyond the join result itself, what useful property does Sort-Merge Join's output have that Hash Partition Join's output lacks?
options: The output is already sorted on the join key, so a downstream operator that wants that order pays no extra sort
The output is deduplicated, so DISTINCT comes free
The output is smaller, because SMJ drops non-matching rows earlier than HPJ
The output is partitioned across disks for parallel reads
questions.explanation: SMJ's merge walks two sorted runs in lockstep, so results stream out in join-key order — a following GROUP BY or ORDER BY on (a prefix of) that key is free. Both algorithms produce the same rows for an inner join; SMJ doesn't deduplicate (a key with m and n matches emits the full m × n cross-product for that group).

questions.question: For a fixed join, raising the write cost C_w from 1 to 10 inflates the SMJ and HPJ costs but leaves BNLJ untouched. Why?
options: BNLJ writes its intermediates to RAM instead of disk
SMJ and HPJ must write intermediate data (sorted runs, partition files) to disk, while BNLJ only ever reads the base tables
BNLJ batches its writes into 64 MB pages, amortizing the cost to zero
The optimizer caps BNLJ's cost at the buffer size regardless of C_w
questions.explanation: BNLJ is a pure-read algorithm: it scans blocks of the outer and re-scans the inner, never materializing intermediate files, so C_w never enters its formula. SMJ writes sorted runs during BigSort and HPJ writes partition files, so expensive writes widen BNLJ's lead — one reason BNLJ wins once the buffer is large.

questions.question: Sweeping buffer size B for the same 100 GB × 1 TB join: at B = 10 pages HPJ wins, but at B = 10,000 pages BNLJ wins. What explains the crossover?
options: HPJ's cost grows linearly with B, so big buffers make partitioning expensive
BNLJ becomes cache-oblivious at large B, eliminating all IO
HPJ's cost is flat (~3 passes regardless of B), while BNLJ's rescans of the inner table shrink dramatically as more of the outer table fits per block
At large B, sort-merge join subsumes BNLJ, so the optimizer relabels it
questions.explanation: HPJ is roughly one read plus one write plus one read no matter how big the buffer is, so its cost stays flat; BNLJ's cost is dominated by ⌈P(outer)/B⌉ inner-table scans, which collapse as B grows (2.6M IOs at B=10 down to 18K at B=10,000). HPJ's cost doesn't grow with B — it just stops being the cheapest option.
